teaser.en: When the sun sets during Ramadan, many Digo households break the fast the traditional way: with a date.

summary.en: *Mtende*, the date palm, is a feather palm that is only occasionally planted on the coast; most dates are imported. Its fruit, *tende*, holds a special place at the table during Ramadan.

about.en:
*Mtende* is a feather palm with a rough trunk patterned by the bases of old leaves and a crown of stiff, grey-green, feather-shaped fronds. The lower leaflets are hardened into sharp spines.

Male and female flowers grow on separate trees, and only the female trees bear fruit: heavy hanging bunches of dates, the *tende*, which ripen from yellow or red to brown.

where.en: It is only occasionally planted on the south coast, and the dates sold in local markets are mostly imported. The humid coast suits it less well than the dry lands where dates are grown commercially.

uses.en: Dates are eaten especially when breaking the Ramadan fast, at sunset, before the evening meal.

culture.en: In a largely Muslim community, *tende* are closely linked to Ramadan, when it is customary to break the day's fast with a date.

names.en: The Mgombato dictionary gives *mtende* for the date palm, and Pakia records the fruit as *tende*. The Swahili names are the same: *mtende* for the palm and *tende* for the fruit. In English it is the date palm, and its scientific name is *Phoenix dactylifera*.

reason.en: Same genus: the wild date palm

sources: Mwalonya, Nicolle, Nicolle & Zimbu, Mgombato: Digo-English-Swahili Dictionary (BTL / Digo Language and Literacy Project, 2004; e-version 2005)

Pakia, M. (2005) African Traditional Plant Knowledge Today: An ethnobotanical study of the Digo at the Kenya Coast. PhD diss., Univ. Bayreuth (Appendix III & Table G.2) https://epub.uni-bayreuth.de/881/1/Pakia.pdf
